124	  groupings.

126	  choices.
127

129	
130	SCOPe combines manual curation with validated automated classification.
131	Automation is useful for placing new structures into established regions of
132	the hierarchy. Manual curation remains important for new folds and
133	superfamilies, remote relationships, artifacts, boundary corrections,
134	heterogeneity, and large complexes.
135	
136	Do not equate automated classification with low quality. Report automated
137	status when it affects provenance or interpretation.
138	
139	## Epistemic Boundaries
140

142

144	2. **SCOPe interpretation:** follows from the retrieved hierarchy and

Verified SCOPe facts (release 2.08, stable 2.08-stable, current public release). All three groups are classified in the same superfamily, b.6.1 "Cupredoxins" (sunid 49503), within fold b.6 "Cupredoxin-like" (sunid 49502), class b (All beta proteins, sunid 48724). They are three distinct sibling families: b.6.1.1 "Plastocyanin/azurin-like" (sunid 49504; family comment "mono-domain proteins"; e.g. plastocyanin domain d1iuza_, sunid 22861, annotated "complexed with cu, so4"), b.6.1.5 "Ephrin ectodomain" (sunid 74874; e.g. ephrin-B2 ectodomain d1ikop_, sunid 71243, mouse; family also contains Ephrin-a5, sunid 110105), and b.6.1.6 "Peptidylarginine deiminase Pad4, N-terminal domain" (sunid 110107; e.g. d5n0ya1, 5n0y A:3-112, sunid 334520, human, an automated match to d1wd8a2). Pairwise lineage comparison of d1iuza_, d1ikop_ and d5n0ya1 in the same release gives lowest shared node b.6.1 (superfamily) for every pair, with no homology warnings or heterogeneity flags on the superfamily, the three families, or the three domains. The b.6.1 superfamily carries the comment "contains copper-binding site". The b.6 fold has one other superfamily, b.6.2 "Major surface antigen p30, SAG1" (sunid 74877), which is NOT in the cupredoxin superfamily and is not asserted homologous to any of the three. Other b.6.1 families include b.6.1.2 (periplasmic domain of cytochrome c oxidase subunit II), b.6.1.3 (multidomain cupredoxins), b.6.1.4 (nitrosocyanin), b.6.1.7 (SO1698-like) and b.6.1.0 (automated matches).

Interpretation (SCOPe hierarchy semantics). Despite their unrelated biology (photosynthetic/respiratory electron transfer, receptor-tyrosine-kinase ligand signalling, and a non-catalytic N-terminal module of a citrullinating enzyme), SCOPe asserts probable common ancestry among them at the superfamily level: same fold AND same superfamily, different families. This is the homology-bearing level, so the relationship is stronger than mere fold similarity (which alone would carry no SCOPe homology claim) but weaker than a shared family (no detectable sequence similarity or shared function is implied). The curators flag the remote nature of the ephrin and PAD4 placements with the qualifier "probably related to cupredoxins" (ephrin: "eukaryotic signaling domain probably related to cupredoxins but lacking the metal-binding site"; PAD4 N-terminal: "probably related to cupredoxins but lacking the metal-binding site"). These are two separate superfamily-level hypotheses by curators, not a demonstration of a single ancestral copper protein.

Should copper binding or electron transfer be inferred? No. (1) SCOPe superfamily membership supports common ancestry, not conserved biochemical function, ligand, or mechanism; the skill's evidence gates forbid inferring a specific ligand or reaction from superfamily placement. (2) SCOPe itself contradicts the transfer: the superfamily-level note "contains copper-binding site" is a description of the classic cupredoxins, and the ephrin (b.6.1.5) and PAD4 N-terminal (b.6.1.6) family annotations explicitly state that these domains LACK the metal-binding site. Copper binding (type-1 Cu site with His/Cys/His/Met-type ligands in plastocyanin/azurin) and the electron-transfer role that depends on it are therefore properties of the Plastocyanin/azurin-like family (and other true cupredoxin families such as b.6.1.2/b.6.1.3), not of the superfamily as a whole. Ephrin ectodomains function as Eph-receptor-binding signalling ligands, and the PAD4 N-terminal domain is a non-catalytic module (PAD4's catalytic domain is separately classified in d.126.1.5 and its middle domain in b.2.9.1), so neither should be annotated as a copper protein or redox carrier. (3) The relationship is a greek-key beta-sandwich scaffold inherited by divergent evolution with loss (or never-acquired) metal-site residues in the eukaryotic lineages; the lacking metal site itself shows function was not conserved. (4) The absence of SCOPe homology warnings is not positive evidence for either homology strength or function; and classification of some PAD4 N-terminal domains (e.g. d5n0ya1) as automated matches means their placement was propagated by sequence from a curated representative (d1wd8a2), which affects provenance but not interpretation.

What would be needed to go further. Asserting copper binding or redox activity in ephrins or PAD4 would require independent experimental evidence (metal-content analysis, spectroscopy, electrochemistry) or at minimum structure-based alignment showing the His/Cys/His/Met ligand positions are conserved, which SCOPe records say they are not. Conversely, the three families should not be called convergent or non-homologous either; SCOPe makes a positive (if qualified, "probably related") homology claim at the superfamily level. Plastocyanin/azurin structures are not safe templates for modelling ephrin or PAD4 metal sites or functional surfaces; template use should be restricted to the shared beta-sandwich core and verified by alignment. Any user wanting the historical basis for the "probably related" judgement would need the primary literature; SCOPe exposes only the curator comment, not the rationale.
